# Setup

```{r packages}
pkgs <- c("readr", "dplyr", "tidyr", "stringr", "ggplot2", "scales", "knitr")
missing <- pkgs[!vapply(pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing)) install.packages(missing, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
invisible(lapply(pkgs, library, character.only = TRUE))

DATA_URL  <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lhamo07/Project-03/main/data_final.csv"
DATA_FILE <- "data_final.csv"
OUT_DIR   <- "output"
dir.create(OUT_DIR, showWarnings = FALSE)
if (!file.exists(DATA_FILE)) download.file(DATA_URL, DATA_FILE, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
```

# Group definitions

```{r groups}
DIFF <- c("Architect, software or solutions", "Data scientist", "AI/ML engineer",
          "Applied scientist", "Data engineer", "Cloud infrastructure engineer",
          "Engineering manager", "Senior executive (C-suite, VP, etc.)",
          "Founder, technology or otherwise")
EXEC <- c("Developer, full-stack", "Developer, back-end", "Developer, front-end",
          "Developer, desktop or enterprise applications", "Developer, mobile",
          "Developer, embedded applications or devices", "Developer, QA or test",
          "Developer, game or graphics")
WORKING <- c("Employed", "Independent contractor, freelancer, or self-employed")
```

# Load data

```{r load}
raw <- read_csv(DATA_FILE, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
                locale = locale(encoding = "UTF-8"), show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
dim(raw)
```

# Clean data

```{r clean}
n_raw <- nrow(raw)

df <- raw |>
  filter(str_detect(ResponseId, "^[0-9]+$")) |>
  distinct(ResponseId, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(CompTotal = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(CompTotal)),
         JobSat    = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(JobSat)))
n_valid <- nrow(df)

print(n_valid)


df <- df |>
# Filtered the dataset to include working respondents from the United States of America only

  filter(Employment %in% WORKING, !is.na(DevType),
         Country == "United States of America",
         between(CompTotal, 20000, 1000000))
n_us <- nrow(df)
print(n_us)

roles_long <- df |>
  select(ResponseId, CompTotal, JobSat, DevType) |>
  separate_rows(DevType, sep = ";") |>
  mutate(Role = str_trim(DevType), DevType = NULL,
         SkillGroup = case_when(Role %in% DIFF ~ "Differentiating",
                                Role %in% EXEC ~ "Execution",
                                TRUE ~ NA_character_)) |>
  filter(!is.na(SkillGroup))
print(roles_long)

resp_group <- roles_long |>
  group_by(ResponseId) |>
  summarise(SkillGroup = if (any(SkillGroup == "Differentiating")) "Differentiating" else "Execution",
            .groups = "drop")
tidy <- df |> select(-DevType) |> inner_join(resp_group, by = "ResponseId")

write_csv(tidy,       file.path(OUT_DIR, "data_clean.csv"))
write_csv(roles_long, file.path(OUT_DIR, "data_roles_long.csv"))
```

```{r attrition}

```

`{tibble(Step = c("Raw rows", "Valid, unique ResponseId",}                 "US working professionals with usable pay", "Classified into a skill group"),        Respondents = c(n_raw, n_valid, n_us, nrow(tidy))) |>   kable()`

The raw dataset contained 1036 rows and 40 columns. During data cleaning, rows with invalid ResponseId values were removed and duplicate ResponseId values were eliminated, leaving 1,033 valid, unique respondents.The dataset was then filtered to include working professionals in the United States of America with annual total compensation (CompTotal) between \$20000 and \$1000000, which left 191 respondents. DevType role were classified into two groups: Differentiating and Execution.Respondents whose roles did not match either group were excluded, leaving a final sample of 168 respondents.

```{r summary}
summary_tbl <- tidy |>
  group_by(SkillGroup) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            median_comp = median(CompTotal),
            mean_comp   = round(mean(CompTotal)),
            mean_jobsat = round(mean(JobSat, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            n_jobsat    = sum(!is.na(JobSat)),
            .groups = "drop")
write_csv(summary_tbl, file.path(OUT_DIR, "summary_by_group.csv"))
kable(summary_tbl, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The summary table shows differences in compensation and job satisfaction between the Differentiating and Execution skill groups. The Differentiating group included 43 respondents and the Execution group included 125. Median compensation was **32.6%** higher in the Differentiating group (**183,000 vs. 138,000**), and mean job satisfaction was also higher (**8.00 vs. 7.28**, based on 31 and 118 responses respectively). These findings support our argument that skill value is associated with organizational differentiation rather than routine execution.

# Plot theme

```{r theme}
COL <- c(Differentiating = "#2563c4", Execution = "#d9822b")
theme_proj <- theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1f2937"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#6b7280"),
        axis.text = element_text(color = "#6b7280"),
        axis.title = element_text(color = "#6b7280"),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank())
```

# Graph 1

```{r graph1, fig.height=6}
g1 <- roles_long |>
  mutate(Role = str_replace(Role, "^Developer, (.*)$", "\\1 developer"))|>
  group_by(Role, SkillGroup) |>
  summarise(median_comp = median(CompTotal), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 5)
p1 <- ggplot(g1, aes(median_comp / 1000, reorder(Role, median_comp), fill = SkillGroup)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("$%.0fk  (n=%d)", median_comp / 1000, n)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.3, color = "#1f2937") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = COL) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.22))) +
  labs(title = "Median pay by role: differentiating vs. execution",
       subtitle = "US respondents, roles with n>=5. Respondents with several roles appear in each.",
       x = "Median annual compensation (USD thousands)", y = NULL) +
  theme_proj +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#e5e7eb"))
ggsave(file.path(OUT_DIR, "graph1_comp_by_role.png"), p1,
       width = 9.5, height = 6, dpi = 180, bg = "white")
p1
```

The bar chart of median pay by role (differentiating vs. executions) shows median annual compensation for the eight roles with at least five US respondents. Compensation varied widely, from **\$88k** for front-end developers **(n = 11)** to **\$240k** for mobile developers **(n = 5)**. Among Differentiating roles, Engineering managers **(\$213k, n = 11)** and software or solutions architects **(\$175k, n = 13)** ranked second and third overall. Both earned more than every Execution role with ten or more respondents, including back-end (\$155k, n = 28) and full-stack developers (\$135k, n = 65).

Mobile developers and applied scientists do not fit the overall pattern. Each has only five respondents. Mobile developers (Execution) have the highest pay of all roles at \$240k. Applied scientists (Differentiating) earn \$130k, the same as desktop and enterprise developers and less than back-end and full-stack developers. With so few respondents, one or two individuals can shift a median sharply, so we treat both as unstable estimates.

# Graph 2

```{r graph2}
g2 <- tidy |>
  filter(!is.na(JobSat)) |>
  mutate(Band = cut(JobSat, c(-Inf, 6, 8, Inf),
                    labels = c("Low (0-6)", "Medium (7-8)", "High (9-10)"))) |>
  group_by(Band, SkillGroup) |>
  summarise(median_comp = median(CompTotal), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

p2 <- ggplot(g2, aes(Band, median_comp / 1000, fill = SkillGroup)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.68) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("$%.0fk\nn=%d", median_comp / 1000, n)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), vjust = -0.3,
            size = 3.2, color = "#1f2937") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = COL) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
  labs(title = "Pay and satisfaction by skill group",
       subtitle = "US respondents with reported satisfaction. Role group is a proxy for task type.",
       x = "Job satisfaction band (JobSat, 0-10)",
       y = "Median annual compensation (USD thousands)") +
  theme_proj +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#e5e7eb"),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
ggsave(file.path(OUT_DIR, "graph2_satisfaction_vs_comp.png"), p2,
       width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 180, bg = "white")
p2
```

In all three job satisfaction bands, it clearly shows Differentiating respondents earned more than Execution respondents: \$168k vs. \$132k (low), \$178k vs. \$150k (medium), and \$250k vs. \$130k (high). Pay rose with satisfaction for Differentiating respondents but stayed roughly flat for Execution respondents. This is consistent with our argument that differentiating work is both better paid and more satisfying.
